Amistad Dam and Reservoir
2.25 General. Amistad (the Spirit of Friendship) Reservoir, stretching 78 miles northwest along the Rio Grande, 14 miles north along the Pecos River, and 25 miles north along the Devils River, is an existing international project built and administered jointly by the Governments of the United States and Mexico under the terms of the 1944 Water Treaty. The principal direct benefits accruing from its construction are water conservation, flood control, an increased flat water fishery resource, recreation, and future generation of hydroelectric energy—the proposed action.
2.26 The existing Amistad Dam is an earth and rockfill embankment having a maximum height of about 245 feet. At its conservation pool elevation of 1,117 feet above sea level, the lake has an area of 67,000 acres with a capacity of 3,505,000 acre-feet. The existing project does not presently have a hydroelectric generating system. At the time of construction of Amistad Dam, the power and energy could not be sold at a price which would repay the costs of hydroelectric power facilities; therefore, a power plant was not found self-liquidating and the plant was not built. However, construction of the dam inlcuded, with Congressional approval, features which would permit addition of a power plant at such time as it would be self-liquidating. Upstream of the Amistad Dam, an approach channel leading to power intakes in the face of the dam was excavated into alluvial gravel and limestone prior to the construction of the dam. The intakes contain trashracks, and will have provisions for both emergency closure against flow and bulkhead closure to permit maintenance, repair, and inspection of the intakes and penstocks. Individual steel-lined penstocks for each generating unit were also installed in tunnels excavated beneath the toe of the dam. All penstocks are 14.5 feet in diameter and 308 feet long. The powerhouse site and tailrace channel was also excavated to provide for water discharge from the turbines.
2.27 Amistad Water Quality. The water quality discussion is based upon the quality of water relative to the criteria established by the Texas Water Quality Board (TWQB). The Rio Grande is the main tributary which feeds the reservoir. During a TWQB study (TWQB, undated), the Rio Grarde contributed 51 percent of the total inflow, the Devils River contributed 36 percent, the the remaining 13 percent came from the Pecos River. The flow from the Pecos River has a heavy mineral content of natural origin with high total dissolved solids (TDS), sulfates, and chlorides. The Rio Grande contributes the highest biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), phosphorus, and suspended solids whereas the Devils River flow is high in nitrogen. Average depth integrated values for hydrogen ion concentration (expressed in pH units) was 8.45 and for dissolved oxygen (DO) was 9.9 mg/l (milligrams per liter). The DO levels approach saturation and the pH is within established limits of 7.0-9.0. Sulfates and chlorides were also within established limits of 250 and 150 mg/l respectively. Fecal coliform concentrations were extremely low at all stations, and total suspended solids were considered low in the reservoir and feeder streams. Sediment analyses in the lake indicate that chemical oxygen demand (COD), volatile solids, and kjeldahl nitrogen levels are generally higher in the Devils River arm of the lake.
